BL-428.design:
FILED 2026-08-15 from Ben's sprint-planning ruling. Four spines were offered - building
tiers, chain depth, the ancient tech ladder, settlement scale - and chain depth was taken.

## What the ruling means

Growth is not a separate track. A corp's reach down the production graph IS its progress:
the deeper the chain it can close, the more the world opens to it. Concretely, a building's
placement precondition becomes a statement about goods the corp can already produce, rather
than a flag some other system sets. Build a bloomery, and the smithy becomes placeable
because blooms exist; not because a tech completed.

Why this over the alternatives, in Ben's choice and worth recording: a tier ladder or a tech
ladder is a SECOND system that must be kept in agreement with the economy, and the project
has already paid that reconciliation cost once (BL-155/BL-156 both settling on the same
`condition_set` and neither building it). Chain depth has no second system to desync from -
it is read off the recipe graph that has to exist anyway.

## Why this is the right substrate right now

The ancient arc's resource enum is ALREADY stocked for it and mostly idle. `components.hpp`
carries stone, timber, sand, clay, peat, charcoal, iron_blooms, grain, fodder, salt and
bullion - the BL-286 logistics tranche plus the ambient raws - and BL-286's own comment
admits the behaviours were never filed ("behaviour unfiled" appears five times). Several
carry no base price in `world_gen.lua`, which is exactly the minable-but-unsellable asymmetry
BL-340 closed for the space tier and never closed for the ancient one.

So the depth ladder does not need new resources. It needs the chains that consume the ones
already sitting in the enum. That is the cheapest possible version of this feature and the
most honest: it retires orphans instead of minting them.

## What has to be defined

1. **A depth metric.** Depth of a good = longest input path back to a raw. Computed once at
   registry load from `recipes.lua`, not authored per good, so it cannot drift from the graph.
   Determinism: the graph is authored data, the walk is pure - it must produce the same
   number on every toolchain (the BL-406 lesson: never let an unordered container decide a
   number the economy reads).
2. **What depth gates.** First cut: building placement. A building type declares the minimum
   depth its corp must have REACHED (i.e. actually produced at least once, recorded per corp),
   and `placement_rules.cpp` enforces it alongside terrain.
3. **Cycles.** The graph must be acyclic for depth to be defined. The registry load should
   reject a cyclic recipe set loudly rather than looping - a headless harness assertion.
4. **What "reached" means for a corp** - produced once ever, or currently producing? Produced
   once ever is the legible choice (progress does not evaporate when a building idles) and
   costs one per-corp bitset over resource_type.

## Guard

A headless harness (`tools/verify/chain_depth.cpp`) asserting: the graph is acyclic; every
good's depth is stable across two loads; every building's declared minimum depth is
REACHABLE from the starting position (no unplaceable building, the roster equivalent of an
orphan resource); and that a fresh corp can reach the deepest tier by some path.

## The refinement seam this leaves open

Tech (BL-296) and politics (BL-158/v0.1.6) refine this rather than gate it: a tech can make a
chain cheaper, shorter, or unlock an ALTERNATE method (BL-430) for a chain you already run -
it does not hand you a depth you did not earn. Stated here so the later systems have a shape
to attach to instead of re-litigating the spine.
BL-428.resolution: Complete 2026-08-16 (slice 2; slice 1, the metric, landed 2026-08-15 with BL-429/430/431). The gate: recipe_required_depth (a recipe's deepest input, derived in the same bounded fixed point as depth_of so it cannot drift from the graph or the era mask), corporation_component::produced_ever + corp_reached_depth (produced-once-ever, never cleared — progress must not evaporate when a building idles), mark_produced at the two sites a good is genuinely made, and refusal at BOTH doors: construct_building and try_switch_recipe. Guarding only placement would have left a one-click bypass (place the shallowest method, retool to the deepest sibling), so the gate is applied at the retool path too; both map to corp_command_result::rejected_depth_locked so the seam cannot tell them apart. ANCIENT ROSTER ONLY per Ben's 2026-08-16 ruling, with the band check on the RECIPE — an any-band recipe stays ungated even in an ancient campaign, so no existing industrial campaign changes shape. Build door filters locked methods out; the Method page disables the Switch with a plain-language reason rather than a depth integer. Guard: chain_depth G1-G4 (11 assertions), including BL-432's no-stranded-building row — the ancient ladder climbs to depth 3 with nothing stranded. Doc: PRODUCTION.md § The gate. Found en route and fixed: the Build door passed a browse recipe index as an absolute id (NR-254), a latent wrong-recipe bug in exactly the ancient campaigns this work targets.
BL-428.summary: RULING 2026-08-15 (Ben, elicitation form): the growth track's spine is CHAIN DEPTH, not building tiers, not the tech ladder, not settlement scale. A corp advances by reaching further down the production graph - the goods it can actually make gate the buildings it may place next - so growth is a consequence of the economy it has built rather than a parallel unlock system laid over it. This is the item the roster expansion (BL-429) and the alternate methods (BL-430) both hang from, and the structure tech (BL-296) and politics (BL-158) are meant to REFINE rather than replace.

BL-432.design:
FILED 2026-08-15 with the economy-breadth sprint, under CLAUDE.md § "Tool creation is skill
creation" - a roster this size will not stay coherent by authorship alone, and the check
written now catches next quarter's orphan.

## Why a harness and not a review pass

BL-286 is the cautionary precedent and it is in the code comments: eleven resource values were
added with "behaviour unfiled", and five of them still have no consumer today, months later.
No human reading a diff catches that; a load-time graph walk catches it in a second. The same
goes for a building nobody can place and a method nobody would ever pick.

## The four assertions

1. **Acyclic.** Depth (BL-428) is undefined on a cycle. Fail loudly at load rather than loop.
2. **No orphans, both directions.** Every `resource_type` is produced by some recipe or
   extractable from some deposit, AND consumed by some recipe or bought by some named actor.
   Terminal goods declare themselves terminal so they are exempt from the second half - an
   explicit exemption list, so an orphan cannot hide as an assumed terminal.
3. **Every building reachable.** For each building's minimum depth, a path exists from a fresh
   corp's starting position to that depth. An unplaceable building is the roster's orphan.
4. **No dominant method.** For each output with alternates, no sibling is better on every axis
   (input cost at reference prices, wage, rate, depth). This is BL-430's design bar mechanised.

## Determinism note

The walk must not depend on container iteration order - the BL-406 lesson, where an unordered
container decided a number the economy read. Sort by authored recipe id before walking, and
assert the depth vector is byte-identical across two loads in the same process.

Runs as `tools/verify/chain_depth.cpp` under the `verifier-headless` skill, named in the skill
so it is discoverable, and added to the ctest tier.
BL-432.resolution: Landed 2026-08-16 as the R1/R2 rows of tools/verify/chain_depth.cpp, completing the item — its third assertion (every building's minimum depth reachable) had already landed as G3 with BL-428's gate, and the first (acyclicity) as D4. R1 (no orphan resources, either direction) SHIPS RED on eight resources and is left that way deliberately: five (grain, fodder, salt, transport_capacity, bullion) are orphaned in both directions and are exactly the BL-286 'behaviour unfiled' values this item's own design predicted, reproduced independently rather than asserted; three more (platinum_group_metals, regolith, machinery) are obtainable but unconsumed. Content decision logged as NR-257. R2 (no dominant method) resolved NR-243's four red pairs WITHOUT changing any recipe magnitude: measured against the axis scripts/recipes.lua already states in its own comments, three pairs have disjoint raws (supply routes, where deposit access rather than price decides) and the fourth differs by a placement precondition, so all four were artefacts of grouping by (primary output, era). Every sibling pair is now bucketed as supply route / precondition / genuine interchangeable method, and only the third is price-compared; the duplicate guard in recipe_switch_harness was deleted rather than left as a second answer, and that harness now runs ALL PASS. Current reading: 4 sibling pairs — 3 supply routes, 1 precondition, 0 interchangeable methods, so the dominance half guards an empty set until BL-430's own alternates are authored (NR-258). BL-433.design:
FOUND 2026-08-15 while measuring the roster for BL-429.

## What is there

`economy.lua` § buildings carries `launchpad` as one of seven building_type entries.
`recipes.lua` id 1 is petroleum -> refined_fuel, and the BL-308 propellant recipes sit on top
of it. The space arc is parked at the ROADMAP/backlog level (~41 items carry `parked: true`),
but parking was a backlog operation and the Lua data was not part of it.

## Why it matters more than it looks

Three ways it bites, in order of how much:

1. **The player at 0 CE can be offered a launchpad.** Whatever the placement rules do in
   practice, the roster is what the Build door reads, and an anachronism there reads as a bug
   in the product rather than a parked feature.
2. **BL-429's roster count is measured against a polluted baseline.** "Seven building types"
   includes one that should not be in this arc at all - so the real ancient roster is six.
3. **The AI scorer sees them.** `corp_ai.cpp` scores build candidates over the roster it is
   given; a rival that builds toward a space chain in an ancient world is not a strategy, it
   is a data leak.

## The call this needs

Not mine to take, because it decides how the two arcs share one data set:

a) **Era-gate the data** - each building and recipe declares the era it belongs to; the
   loader filters on the campaign's era. Truest, and ERAS.md already designs an era system
   (status: designed, NOT implemented), so this would be its first real consumer.
b) **Split the data files** - `economy_ancient.lua` / `economy_space.lua`, chosen at startup.
   Cheapest, and honest about the two arcs being two products; costs duplication where they
   genuinely overlap (extraction_site, port, warehouse).
c) **Leave it and rely on placement rules** - the status quo. Cheapest of all and the reason
   this was invisible until now.

RECOMMENDATION: (a). It is the same amount of work as (b) once, it gives ERAS.md its first
implementation instead of leaving it a designed-but-unbuilt doc, and the ancient arc's own
tech ladder (BL-296) will want an era-ish gate anyway. But it is a shared-substrate decision
and BL-429 should not start before it is answered - the roster expansion writes into exactly
these files.

## RULING 2026-08-15: option (a), era-gate the data

Taken on Ben's instruction to answer this myself and start Sprint 17. Reasons unchanged from
the recommendation: (a) and (b) cost about the same once, (a) gives ERAS.md its first
implementation instead of leaving it a designed-but-unbuilt doc, and BL-296's ancient tech
ladder will want an era-shaped gate anyway. (b) additionally duplicates every entry the two
arcs genuinely share — extraction_site, port, warehouse — and duplication is what goes stale.

## The trap that shapes the implementation

A recipe's **id is its index** in `m_recipes`, and that id is STORED in
`building_component.recipe`. So the era filter must be a MASK, never a removal: dropping a
disallowed recipe from the vector would silently repoint every building whose recipe sat
after it. `recipes.lua`'s own header already says "keep the order stable so authored ids
hold" — the filter has to honour that.

The shape that satisfies both, without touching the ten call sites that iterate recipes:

  * `m_recipes` keeps EVERY authored recipe, in file order. `get_recipe(id)` and
    `recipe_id(name)` stay absolute — they are the storage/lookup path.
  * A new `m_allowed` vector holds the positions permitted in the current era.
    `recipe_count(bt)` / `recipe_at(bt, i)` map through it — they are the BROWSE path, and
    every existing caller already means "the recipes available to me" by them.

That split is why no consumer needs rewriting: the ten sites that walk
`[0, recipe_count)` start walking the era's recipes instead of all of them, which is what
each of them was already trying to express.

## Band, not era-number

Two bands plus a wildcard: `any` / `ancient` / `industrial`. Deliberately NOT reusing
ERAS.md's Era 0 / Era 1 numbering — that axis is about *space access within the industrial
arc* and is gated on launchpad presence, a different question from *which product is this*.
Conflating them would give one field two meanings.

The campaign's band is derived from `world_params::epoch_year` against the SAME 1700
threshold the antiquity branch already documents, so there is one number in the codebase and
not two: below 1700 is ancient, 1700 and above is industrial.

## Default is 'any', and that is load-bearing

An unset registry permits everything, so every existing headless harness — none of which
knows about eras — loads exactly the roster it loads today. Same property BL-409 relied on
for spectator mode: the new behaviour is opt-in, so the un-opted path is byte-identical and
can be asserted as such.
BL-433.resolution: Landed 2026-08-15, option (a). `era_band` (any/ancient/industrial) tags every authored building type and recipe; the campaign's band is derived from world_params::epoch_year against the 1700 threshold and set in app::load_economy. The filter MASKS rather than removes, which is the whole shape of the change: storage (get_recipe/recipe_id) stays absolute so stored recipe ids never repoint, while browse (recipe_count/recipe_at) walks the era's list — and because every existing caller of the browse path already meant 'the recipes available to me', none of the ten call sites needed rewriting. construct_building is the authoritative gate (construction_result::era_locked, distinct from tech_locked because no research reaches it, surfaced as corp_command_result::rejected_era_locked rather than overloading rejected_placement — BL-395's complaint); the Selection build door filters on building_available so it does not offer what the gate would refuse. Default band is `any`, so every pre-existing harness and the default world are untouched. Guard: tools/verify/era_roster.cpp, 15 assertions ALL PASS, live-Lua and script-rooted. Docs: PRODUCTION.md gained an era-band section (incl. the storage/browse table); ERAS.md's header block gained the note that this is a SECOND thing in code saying 'era' and is a different axis from Era 0/Era 1. Ancient roster is deliberately thin (steel, food_rations, refined_copper) — filling it out is BL-429.

BL-434.design:
FILED 2026-08-16 mid-playtest. Ben: "Now is also the time to implement the building splits, so
Processing Facility doesn't just do the job of every type of processing, allowing simple
splits. It should also cost money for any building to undergo a large change, making it in
some cases cheaper to just build another."

First cut: add `recipe::group`, tag every recipes.lua entry, collapse the Build door's
per-recipe processing rows into one row per group, and price a cross-group recipe switch at
a steep multiplier (`cross_group_multiplier`, first-cut 6.0x) on top of BL-430's existing
switch cost — cheap to retool within a group, expensive enough to often favour building fresh
across groups.

## RETRACTION, same session

Ben reconsidered after the priced version landed: "I didn't realise that switching methods
can mean changing to a different building type — we should retire that completely. So the
only way to access a different building type is fully dismantling the building, then using
the tile selector to reselect and build a new building." Cross-group switching is not merely
expensive now, it does not exist: `try_switch_recipe` refuses a cross-group target outright
(`recipe_switch_result::cross_group`, mutates nothing), the Method page's candidate list only
ever offers same-group recipes (never shows what it would refuse), and
`cross_group_multiplier` was removed rather than left unused. Dismantle + rebuild via the
tile selector is the sole route to change a building's group.

BL-435.design:
FILED 2026-08-16, from a live look at an autostarted campaign whose player corp
held no processing facility at all — so the Method page (BL-430/BL-431's whole
surface) had nothing to show, and the chain-depth ladder (BL-428) had no rung to
stand on.

## The measurement that prompted it

`tools/verify/player_seed_sweep.cpp` (written the same session) over 24 seeds,
12 warm ticks:

  * 11/24 hand the player a corp with at least one processing facility.
  * 13/24 give a PURE-EXTRACTION corp — no processing at all.
  * 3 of those (seeds 9, 12, 22) give no production building of any kind.
  * Solvency is NOT the discriminator: every one of the 24 seeds ends positive
    (1.3k - 55k cr) and not one dips below zero on the way.

That last line matters, because the instinct was to filter on profitability. The
economy is not producing broke openings; it is producing SHALLOW ones.

## Why a selection screen rather than a seed filter

The obvious fix — reject seeds whose player corp lacks a processor — is a hidden
constraint that makes the world generator quietly lie about its own distribution,
and it throws away half the seeds to fix a problem that is really about WHICH corp
in the world the player is handed. Every one of those 13 worlds contains plenty of
corporations with processing facilities; the player was simply assigned a poor one.

`docs/generation/CORPORATION_GENERATION.md` already carries the deferred
"corporation selection screen" as an open item. This is that item, now with a
measured reason to exist: it converts an invisible seed lottery into a stated
choice, and it is the honest version of the fix (the player sees the opening
positions and picks, rather than the generator silently discarding worlds).

## Shape

1. After generation, present the campaign's corporations as selectable openings —
   name, home nation, industrial focus, starting assets by type, opening balance.
2. The player picks; `world::player_entity` is set from the choice rather than by
   the generator's own assignment.
3. A "surprise me" option keeps the current behaviour for players who want it.
4. The New World wizard (docs/ui/STARTUP.md) is the natural host — a stage between
   generation completing and Begin.

## Interaction with the sweep

`player_seed_sweep` stays a REPORTING tool either way: once selection exists, its
"no processing facility" column stops being a rejection reason and becomes a
description of one candidate among several. Worth keeping as the guard that the
generator still produces a spread of openings worth choosing between.

## Deliberately not doing

Rejection-sampling seeds at generation time, or shipping a hard-coded whitelist of
"good" seeds. Both hide the distribution rather than exposing it, and the second
would rot the moment generation changes.

The fix is to stop assigning the player a corp by lottery and let them choose from the world's own corporations, which is the deferred corporation selection screen CORPORATION_GENERATION.md already names.

BL-437.design:
FILED 2026-08-16 out of BL-436's measurement chain. BL-436 asked why refining does not pay; R3 said processors starve; R4 asked what they starve ON, and the answer is much larger than the question.

## The measurement (tier_margin R4, 3 seeds x 20 ticks, real generated world)

  id  resource                tiles   sites   units/tick
   0  iron_ore                55466      44     75478.3
   6  agricultural_produce    12315      30      5047.3
   7  water                   14042       5      1556.0
   3  silica                  21881      10       557.9
   2  petroleum                2756       2       515.0
  12  timber                   5404      11       385.1
   4  copper_ore              17445       3       305.6
  11  stone                   83461       8       164.5
   1  coal                     1671       0         0.0   <-- MINED BY NOTHING
   5  rare_earth_ore          10373       0         0.0   <--
   8  iron_nickel_ore           330       0         0.0   <--
   9  platinum_group_metals     117       0         0.0   <--
  10  regolith                16361       0         0.0   <--
  13  sand                     1601       0         0.0   <--
  14  clay                     2146       0         0.0   <--
  15  peat                     4358       0         0.0   <--

Eight of the sixteen mineable raws are produced in ZERO quantity, and every one is named as an input by at least one authored recipe. Iron ore alone out-produces everything else combined by two orders of magnitude.

## The cause, and it is one function

placement_rules::richest_extractable walks k_extractable and returns the resource with the highest resource_deposit value on that tile. One tile, one resource, winner takes all. Iron ore is on 55,466 tiles - more than any raw except stone - so on almost any tile worth siting a mine on, iron ore is the pick. A resource that is never the richest on any tile is unreachable by construction. The deposits are there in quantity; the SELECTION rule is what excludes them.

## Why priority A: it is upstream of several filed problems

  * BL-436 (processing does not pay): `steel` is the era-aware DEFAULT recipe and needs coal as its reagent. Nothing mines coal, so the default recipe can NEVER run - most of the 34.9% starvation R3 measured, with coal alone at 38.5% of all starved ticks.
  * BL-428's chain depth asks the player to climb a graph whose lower rungs cannot be supplied.
  * BL-429/BL-430's ancient roster consumes peat, clay and sand - all three unmined - so a large part of that content is unreachable in play.
  * BL-435's selection screen presents corps with processors as richer openings when those processors may have no possible input.

## Options, none costed

  A) A site targets a resource CHOSEN AT PLACEMENT (by the builder, or by what the local market lacks) rather than by richest-deposit. Most faithful to the design - a mine is sited FOR something - and it makes the Build door a real decision. Largest change: corp_ai, corporation_generation and the player build path all pick targets via richest_extractable today.
  B) One site works SEVERAL deposits on its tile, so a tile's coal is reachable alongside its iron. Smallest code change; weakens the tile-choice decision.
  C) Bias richest_extractable by scarcity or unmet demand rather than raw richness. Cheapest, but a heuristic patch on a rule whose problem is that it is a heuristic.

MEASURE BEFORE CHOOSING (BL-436's own lesson): check whether the eight are never the richest ANYWHERE, or merely never on the tiles corps actually site on. Different problems - B only fixes the second.

## Guarded by

tier_margin R4's assertion - 'every recipe input that has deposits is mined by at least one site' - fails today naming the count (8), and passes when this lands.

Iron ore gets 44 sites and 75,478 units/tick - more than every other resource combined by two orders of magnitude. Cause: placement_rules::richest_extractable gives a site the single richest deposit on its tile, so a resource never richest anywhere is never mined, however many tiles carry it and however badly a recipe needs it. MEASURED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call: run the never-richest-anywhere measurement before costing any option). tier_margin R5 reports, per resource, the share of tiles carrying it on which it is the RICHEST - i.e. how often richest_extractable would actually return it. Computed with the real function, not a reimplementation.

  id  resource                tiles  richest   win%  sites
  10  regolith                16361    15644  95.6%      0
   8  iron_nickel_ore           330      220  66.7%      0
   5  rare_earth_ore          10373     1273  12.3%      0
  15  peat                     4358       56   1.3%      0
   1  coal                     1671       19   1.1%      0
   9  platinum_group_metals     117        1   0.9%      0
  13  sand                     1601        2   0.1%      0
  14  clay                     2146        0   0.0%      0
  (for contrast: water 100%, silica 74.5%, agri 70.0%, iron_ore 38.6% - all mined)

THIS CORRECTS THIS ITEM AS FILED. The filing treated all eight as one problem caused by one rule. They are THREE problems:

  1. OFF-WORLD REACH, not the rule: regolith (95.6% win) and iron_nickel_ore (66.7%) are the richest almost everywhere they occur and still have zero sites. The rule would happily return them; nothing mines them because no corp operates on airless bodies or metallic asteroids in Era 0. That is the era gate working as designed and is NOT in this item's scope. Two of the eight are therefore expected, and the headline 'eight raws mined by nothing' overstated the defect.
  2. OUT-RANKED IN PRACTICE, and this is the real item: coal 1.1%, rare_earth_ore 12.3%, peat 1.3%, sand 0.1%, PGM 0.9%. They are present on thousands of tiles but something outranks them almost everywhere, so in practice richest_extractable never returns them. 'Never richest anywhere' turned out to be the wrong question - the win RATE is what matters, and a binary richest-somewhere/never test would have given a confidently wrong answer for coal.
  3. NEVER RICHEST: clay alone, at 0.0%.

WHAT THIS DOES TO THE OPTIONS. Option B (one site works several deposits on its tile) now looks much stronger than when filed: groups 2 and 3 are precisely the case where the resource COEXISTS with a richer one on the same tile, so working several deposits reaches all of them - coal, sand, peat, clay and rare_earth in one change. It does nothing for group 1, but group 1 does not need it. Option A remains the most faithful to the design and is still the larger change. Option C is now the weakest: biasing the winner still picks exactly one resource per tile, so it would unblock coal only by starving whatever it displaced.

THE COAL CASE IS THE URGENT ONE regardless of which option wins: `steel` is the era-aware default recipe, coal is its reagent, and coal is mined nowhere - so the DEFAULT recipe can never run in a shipped campaign. That single fact is most of BL-436's starvation.

BL-441.design:
Register the WANT alongside the FILL. run_processing already computes the full-run need per input before deciding coverage (economy_system.cpp, the BL-130 pool + inventory coverage loop) — that figure is the demand, and it is already in hand at exactly the point the shortfall is known. It must reach mc.demand whether or not the draw succeeded.

Two things to keep straight, because conflating them is how this defect reads as correct: SUPPLY is an offer and INVENTORY is a delivery (the distinction BL-422 landed and MARKETS.md records). Demand needs the same split — what was WANTED versus what was BOUGHT. The purchase record (auto_buys, the VWAP accumulator, the money actually paid) must keep reading the FILL; only the price-resolution input changes to the want. Paying for goods nobody delivered would be BL-422 s defect in the opposite direction.

Determinism: the want must be accumulated in a deterministic order — this is the same seam where BL-422 found a latent unordered_map float-accumulation nondeterminism, so accumulate over a sorted key set, not a hash order.

GUARD, and it must be shown to fail on the pre-change build: a processor starved of an input registers demand equal to its full-run NEED, not to the quantity it managed to draw; and a resource with real demand and no supply resolves to the top of the price band rather than to base.
BL-441.summary: Found 2026-08-17 testing Ben's proposal to widen the price band. market_clearing.cpp:601 reads `w.markets.at(mid).demand[r] += qty` where qty is bought[r] — what a corp ACTUALLY BOUGHT. A processor that needed 16 units of an input and could only draw 2 registers demand of 2. The resource therefore reads to resolve_price as one almost nobody wants, its price never rises, and no band width can amplify a signal that is zero. resolve_price ALREADY does the right thing given real numbers — its own line 34 comment reads "demand with no supply — top of the band" — so the pricing mechanism is built and correct; it is being starved of input.
BL-441.consequences_for_shipped_claims:

BL-444.design:
## What the audit measured

Three artefacts already carry the answer, and no tool joins them.

- `src/world/corp_command.hpp` is the authoritative verb list (15, append-only).
- `docs/ai/ACTIONS.json` gameplay family transcribes it (15 entries, complete today).
- Each dictionary entry carries a `surface` field naming its UI press, or saying SEAM-ONLY.
- `src/world/corp_ai.cpp` assigns `cmd.verb` at exactly ten sites, covering eight distinct verbs.

The join is mechanical and cheap. It is not written.

## Shape

A node tool, `tools/session/verb_coverage.js`, emitting one row per verb with four columns:
seam / dictionary / UI press / AI candidate. Sources, in order of authority:

1. Parse the `corp_verb` enum out of `corp_command.hpp` — the seam wins over everything.
2. Read `ACTIONS.json` gameplay entries; a missing verb is a dictionary defect, and per
   BL-270 the dictionary is the wrong one when they disagree.
3. Read each entry `surface` field; a `SEAM-ONLY` marker means no human press. This is the
   one axis read from prose rather than code, and it is deliberate — the prose is the
   maintained record, and a grep of `src/ui` for a verb name finds nothing useful because
   the UI calls seam functions, not verbs.
4. Grep `corp_ai.cpp` for `cmd.verb = corp_verb::X` assignments.

Exit non-zero on a **dictionary** gap only. UI and AI gaps are reported, not failed — they
are legitimate design states (`set_workforce_auto` may well be correctly AI-absent), and a
tool that fails on them would be muted within a week.

## Why it is priority A for its size

It is the instrument the reachability argument rests on. Sprint 22 proposes closing gaps;
without this the closing is unverified and the reopening is unnoticed. Per CLAUDE.md
§ Tool creation is skill creation, it should be wrapped or invoked from an existing skill
rather than left loose.

## WIDENED 2026-08-17 (Ben, on NR-308): add a subsystem column

The four-column join above answers *"is each verb that exists reachable"*. It cannot answer
*"does each subsystem own a verb at all"*, because a join over existing verbs is structurally
blind to the absent one. The Sprint 25 audit found the gap that proves it: the convoy layer —
`supply_system.cpp` plus the whole of `logistics.cpp` plus four rendering paths, and the
only coupling between two markets' prices — owns **zero** of the fifteen verbs, and this
tool as first scoped would have reported a clean sheet over it.

**Shape.** A second table: one row per world subsystem, listing the verbs whose subject
belongs to it and a count. The subsystem list is **authored, not derived** — a hand-kept
list in the tool naming each `src/world` subsystem and its verbs, reviewed when a
subsystem is added. Deriving it from filenames would be clever and wrong: it would silently
grow a row for every new file and mean nothing.

**Reported, never failed.** A subsystem legitimately owning no verb is a real design state —
`market_clearing` should not take player commands. The row exists so the absence is
*visible and deliberate* rather than inferred, which is the same reasoning BL-451 uses for
printing a per-verb histogram it never asserts on.

**Difficulty 2 → 3.** Still small, but it is a second data source and a maintained list.

LANDED 2026-08-19 (Batch Delivery). Built tools/session/verb_coverage.js: Table 1 joins corp_command.hpp's 24-verb seam, ACTIONS.json's dictionary, each entry's surface field (UI press), and corp_ai.cpp's grep-derived AI-candidate set; exits non-zero only on a dictionary gap. Table 2 is an authored per-subsystem verb-ownership map, reported never failed. First real run found a genuine dictionary gap - march_unit/halt_unit/disband_unit (BL-470, appended 2026-08-19) are missing from ACTIONS.json, exit code 1 - logged as NR-373, left open as a follow-up (not this item's scope to close).

BL-448.design:
## Why now

The Sprint 21 proposal audit found that *"the capability everyone assumes exists and does
not is a hostility model"*, and flagged it as a design call filed as work nowhere. Ben
settled the design on 2026-08-17. This is that call, written as an item.

Without it there is no legal predicate on an attack verb, no engagement trigger condition,
and no way for the scorer to price an engagement. It blocks BL-315 (armed house conflict
spine) F2 entirely.

## Naming — do not call it standing

`src/world/standing.{hpp,cpp}` already exists and means something else: the BL-262 coarse
**power** read (negligible / minor / notable / major / dominant) over reach, capital and
market share. Overloading the word would make every future sentence about "a corp
standing" ambiguous between how strong it is and how it feels about you.

Proposed term: **stance**. `corp_stance { friendly, neutral, hostile }`, in
`src/world/stance.{hpp,cpp}`. GLOSSARY.md gets both terms with the distinction stated.

## The substrate that already exists

`world::corp_reputation` is a `std::map<std::pair<entity_id, entity_id>, float>` — already
directed, already serialised, already sorted-key deterministic. A stance table is the same
shape with an enum payload, so the data-model cost is near zero **if stance is directed**.
See the symmetry question below, which is exactly the question of whether it may be.

`condition_set` and `rejected_embargo` also already exist: `request_quote` declines when a
supplier condition set evaluates false against the buyer. So there is already a
relationship-shaped gate in the economy, and stance should feed it rather than sit beside it.

## SETTLED 2026-08-17 (Ben, on NR-302): HYBRID — hostility directed, friendship symmetric

The question was directed (A), symmetric (B), or hybrid. **Ben chose the hybrid**, and the
recommendation on file was A — so this is a deliberate overrule and the reason matters:
the hybrid is the only reading that is honest to *both* halves of the fiction at once.
**You can be attacked without agreeing. You cannot be befriended without agreeing.** A and
B each get one half of that right and the other half wrong.

### What it costs, stated plainly, because this is the most expensive of the three

**Two tables with two different key rules**, and that is the whole of the added cost:

| | Hostility | Friendship |
|---|---|---|
| Key | directed `(actor, target)` | canonicalised `(min id, max id)` |
| Shape | `std::map<std::pair<entity_id,entity_id>, bool>` — same as `corp_reputation` | one row per pair |
| Verb | `declare_hostile` — unilateral, immediate | `offer_friendship` → `accept_friendship` |
| Undo | `return_to_neutral`, unilateral | `return_to_neutral`, unilateral **by either party** |
| One-sided state? | **yes, and it is the point** — an ambush | **impossible by construction** |

### The three invariants this shape needs, and none of them are optional

1. **A pending offer is not a stance.** It lives in its own store, not in the friendship
   table, or an unaccepted offer reads as a friendship to every consumer. Accepting moves
   it; declining or expiring erases it.
2. **Hostility outranks friendship when both exist.** The hybrid makes this reachable —
   A and B are friends (symmetric row) and then A declares hostile (directed row). The
   resolution rule is that **declaring hostility dissolves the friendship row atomically**,
   in the same command, rather than leaving a contradictory pair for consumers to
   arbitrate. A rejected declaration mutates neither table.
3. **Consumers must ask the right question of the right table.** `is_hostile(a, b)` is
   directional and `are_friends(a, b)` is not, and the two must not be collapsed behind a
   single `stance_between()` accessor that hides which is which. That convenience is the
   most likely way this design gets silently flattened back to B.

### What it buys, which is why it is worth the second table

The ambush survives — BL-458 (interdiction) can intercept a convoy belonging to a corp that
does not yet know it is at war, which is the single most characteristic thing a hostile act
can be. And friendship keeps the property that makes it meaningful: it cannot be imposed,
so a friendly row is always evidence that two corps both chose it.

## Scope

World state, the three verbs (`declare_hostile`, `offer_friendship`, `accept_friendship`,
plus a return-to-neutral), serialisation, and a determinism harness. **No consequence** —
stance gates nothing in this item. What hostility permits is BL-315 (armed house conflict
spine); what friendship permits is a later call. Landing the substrate inert is deliberate:
it lets the model be argued about against a real save rather than against prose.
BL-448.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 on Ben's ruling the same date: hostility is a declared war state corps opt into deliberately, with a friend state alongside it - three modes (friend / neutral / hostile) as the substrate for naive diplomacy. Answers the risk Sprint 21 named and left unfiled. SETTLED 2026-08-17 (Ben, on NR-302): the HYBRID reading - hostility stored directed, friendship stored symmetric, two tables with two key rules. Difficulty raised 4 -> 5: it is the most expensive of the three options and carries three non-optional invariants (a pending offer is not a stance; declaring hostility dissolves a friendship row atomically; consumers must not collapse the two tables behind one accessor). [COMPLETE 2026-08-19: src/world/stance.{hpp,cpp} landed — directed corp_hostile_pairs, symmetric corp_friend_pairs, pending corp_friend_offers; four corp_command verbs (declare_hostile, offer_friendship, accept_friendship, return_to_neutral); stance_determinism.cpp 36/36 PASS, in-memory replay only (no serialiser exists — see NR-349). Substrate landed inert per design, no consequence wired yet.]

BL-452.design:
## The gap, measured

`corp_verb` holds fifteen values. Eight name a building, three an order, two a
contract, one a body (`survey`), one a tile (`place_road`). **None names a convoy.**
`dispatch_convoys` is called from the economy tick and from nowhere else; the only
way a player influences a lane is indirectly, by building a port or a road and
hoping the auto-dispatcher notices.

This is the same defect BL-393 (units are write-only and inert) describes one layer
over, and it is larger: the convoy layer is ~340 lines of `supply_system.cpp` plus
the whole of `logistics.cpp`, and it is the *only* coupling between two markets'
prices. SUPPLY.md § Convoy entity states it outright - "there is no abstract
price-coupling term between bodies: the convoy *is* the coupling". The player cannot
touch it.

**Sprint 22's reachability audit could not see this.** It joined seam, dictionary,
surface and scorer over the verbs that exist, and every one of the fifteen is
reachable from at least one direction. The question it did not ask is which
*subsystems* own no verb. Recorded as NR-308.

## Shape - two verbs, not a routing UI

**`dispatch_convoy`** (subject = source market, `target` = resource, `quantity`,
`counterparty` = destination market). Commits cargo from the source pool at once,
exactly as the auto path does, prices the haul through the same `intra_body_path` /
`body_distance_au` call, and appends a `convoy_component`. It is the auto-dispatcher's
body with the shortfall scan removed - **no second code path**, which is the same
mitigation Sprint 22 named for BL-445.

**`hold_convoy`** (subject = convoy). Not a cancel: cargo already left the pool, so
a cancel would have to invent a return leg or mint goods. A held convoy stops
advancing and pays nothing further; releasing it resumes. The narrow version is
the honest one - a full recall is a separate design question and is out of scope here.

Both go through `apply_corp_command` and are refused, not clamped, on a bad field:
the seam is an untrusted input boundary (standing rules, 2026-08-14), so quantity is
range-checked against the source pool as the value that lands, and a rejection
mutates nothing.

## What this deliberately does not add

No waypoint routing, no standing lane orders, no per-node throughput (SUPPLY.md puts
that out of prototype scope), no convoy escort. Escort is the interesting one and it
belongs after BL-315 (conflict spine) and BL-448 (stance) - a convoy cannot be escorted
until something can threaten it.

## Dictionary

Two new `gameplay` family entries in ACTIONS.json, **transcribed from the seam once it
exists** and never authored ahead of it (BL-270's discipline). This is also the first
time the dictionary will carry a verb whose subject is a transient entity, which is
worth getting right: a convoy id is valid for a handful of ticks.

## Why this minor

v0.1.12 (logistics modes) is themed *"distance costs something, in more than one way,
and the player can see it"* and carries four items - freight premium (BL-153), rail
(BL-173), coastal ports (BL-188), supply-lens flow (BL-175). Every one of them makes
distance cost more or read better. **After all four land, the player still cannot
dispatch a convoy.** This item and BL-453 are what turn that minor from a tuning pass
into a lever.
BL-452.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 from the Sprint 25 logistics audit. Layer 5 - convoy component, terrain-weighted A* routing, the km-per-tile travel-time model, road/river/node discounts, four rendering paths and a persistent trade-route store - is entirely automatic. None of the fifteen corp_verbs names a convoy. SUPPLY.md's own Build status has carried the line 'Player-directed dispatch (the Dispatch trigger exception has no UI or code path yet)' since the layer landed, and its Dispatch trigger section describes player-direction as a shipped exception that was never built.

BL-454.design:
## The measured state

`grep w.units` across `economy_system.cpp`, `budget_system.cpp` and `construction.cpp`
returns nothing. `apply_budget`'s five flows (income / expenditure / maintenance /
wages / interest - FINANCE.md) are **all building-derived**. `operating_cost` takes a
`building_component`. There is no unit pass anywhere in the economy tick.

So the standing rules' concern about rival hiring - BL-324's "never on cash" for
availability, and Ben's 2026-08-13 ruling that spending is still gated by solvency -
currently prices only the **moment of hire**. A rival that hires twelve units carries
no recurring burden for them, which means the solvency gate it passes at hire time is
the only pressure the roster ever applies.

**The second half of the same gap: `demolish_building` erases the asset, the building
and its stockpile, and never touches `w.units`.** Demolishing a military base silently
orphans every unit mustered there - BL-393 names this and the code confirms it
(`construction.cpp`, the three erase calls).

## SETTLED 2026-08-17 (Ben, on NR-306): reading (c) - credits AND goods

The question was credits (a), goods (b), or both (c). **Ben's answer: both - credits and
military goods (supplies, rations, weapons).** This is the largest of the three and it is
the one that makes the item what its title claims: an army that costs something is an army
that *draws on the network*, not one that debits a number.

Three consequences follow immediately, and none of them are optional under (c):

**1. The cost is a VECTOR, not a float.** The unit pass resolves, per unit type per tick,
a credit wage plus a set of `{resource_type, qty}` draws against the corp's pool **on that
unit's body**. Written as a float-plus-extras it becomes a rewrite the first time a second
good is added; written as a vector from the start the roster carries the data and the pass
carries no per-good knowledge at all.

**2. A pool can be empty, so there is a partial-supply case, so there is a shortfall rule.**
This is the part reading (a) did not have. When the goods are not there the unit must do
*something*, and the honest options are strength decay, desertion (count attrition), or
combat-effectiveness reduction. **Decay is the right one and it is already designed** -
BL-325 S3 is out-of-supply decay, authored as a deterministic scalar in economy.lua with no
RNG. Under (c) the two items converge: S3's decay fires when the unit is beyond the reach
field, this item's fires when the goods did not arrive, and they are the same subtraction
from the same field for the same reason. **Land one decay rule with two triggers, not two
rules.**

**3. The goods have to exist, and one of them does not.** See § The roster gap below.

## The roster gap - there is no military good in the game

Audited against `resource_type` (37 values, RESOURCES.md):

| Ben's word | Nearest existing value | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **rations** | `food_rations` (22) | **exists**, produced from agricultural produce, already consumed by the consumer-goods recipe |
| **supplies** | `medical_supplies` (36) | **exists but is wrong** - it is a *habitability* good consumed by population centres, and borrowing it would make an army compete with a city for medicine on a shared price. Defensible later; not what "military supplies" means |
| **weapons** | *nothing* | **ABSENT.** No ordnance, no small arms, no munitions anywhere in the enum |

So (c) cannot be built as stated without a new terminal good. That is **BL-457**, filed
alongside this item, and this item `requires` it.

The finding is larger than a missing enum value. The 2026-08-10 refocus (NR-120) put the
player's identity as *"a national private militia, which uses private companies to build
equipment"*, with trade *"coloured directly with military use"*. BL-350 gave procurement a
terminal good to contract for and it is `spacecraft_components` - **space hardware. There
is no military terminal object in the roster at all.** The refocus's other half has been
an assertion since the day it was made.

## Slices

**U0 - the good.** BL-457 lands ordnance and its recipe. Blocking; nothing below works
without a good to draw.

**U1 - the unit pass.** A pass over `w.units` in the economy tick, deterministic, iterated
in sorted unit-id order. Resolves the per-type cost vector from the roster, debits credits
and goods, and records the shortfall. Orphan cleanup rides here: a unit whose owning corp
no longer holds a completed military_base on its body is the demolish defect's fix, and the
pass is the only place that can see it.

**U2 - the flow.** Upkeep as its own term in `apply_budget`'s decomposition, not folded
into wages - the budget ledger reads the split and a hidden term is a term nobody tunes.
The goods half is a pool debit, not a budget flow, and shows in the stockpile ledger.

**U3 - the shortfall rule.** One decay rule, two triggers, shared with BL-325 S3 (see
consequence 2 above). Deterministic scalar, no RNG.

**U4 - the surface.** Upkeep on the unit Selection card - credits and the goods vector,
with the unmet part called out - and a force line in the budget ledger. A cost the player
cannot see is a cost they cannot respond to, and under (c) there are now two ways to fail
to pay it.

## The check

A `unit_upkeep` harness asserting: (1) a corp with N units pays exactly N x the type's
credit rate and debits exactly N x each good, and nothing else moves; (2) an empty pool
produces decay at the authored scalar and never negative stock; (3) demolishing the base
leaves no orphan unit; (4) two runs of one seed produce identical balances, pools and
strengths; (5) **the rate-zero run is byte-identical to the pre-item build** - the same
defaults-off proof `spectator_determinism` used for BL-409, and the thing that makes the
golden re-bless honest.

## Risk

This touches `economy_system.cpp` and `economy.lua`, which Sprint 21's own risk paragraph
names as the hot seam. It **moves every economy golden**, because every seed with a hiring
rival now spends differently, and under (c) it also moves every *pool*. Take the
measurement of how far rival balances and stocks move before raising the rate off zero.

**Reading (c) roughly doubles (a)'s cost and adds a genuine design surface** (the shortfall
rule). It is the right answer for what the item is trying to do; it is not the cheap one,
and it should not be promoted as though it were a one-session job.

## Correction to this item's first draft

The 2026-08-17 filing said the goods half was *"the grain/fodder line BL-287 has been
holding"*. Both halves are wrong: BL-287 is a verify-harness item, the logistics-goods item
is **BL-286**, and grain and fodder were **removed** from the enum by NR-257 on 2026-08-16
as produced-by-nothing/consumed-by-nothing. The stale citation was inherited from BL-325's
own design prose, which still carries it (BL-295 fixed the same citation in components.hpp
and did not reach the backlog copy). Recorded as NR-311.
